title: A crystal that turns heat into voltage differently in each direction
hook: Heat this crystal from the left and you get one voltage; heat it from the right and you get another — no magnets involved. Two Weyl semimetals just showed it works at room temperature.
key_points: Thermoelectric materials turn a temperature difference into voltage; normally reversing the gradient just flips the sign.
In low-symmetry crystals a second-order response survives, so the two directions are genuinely not mirror images.
The team measured this in the type-II Weyl semimetals Td-WTe2 and TaIrTe4, up to room temperature.
No magnetic field or magnetic material is needed — the effect comes from the crystal's own reduced symmetry.
They resolved every symmetry-allowed component: nonlinear Seebeck, nonlinear Nernst and mixed-directional effects.
Both Berry curvature and electron scattering contribute, dominating different components of the response.
content_html: A thermoelectric material converts a temperature difference into a voltage — the effect behind thermocouples and waste-heat harvesters. Ordinarily it is a strictly reciprocal business: reverse the temperature gradient and the voltage simply flips sign. But in crystals with low enough symmetry, a second-order term survives that does not flip, meaning heating the sample from one side genuinely is not the mirror image of heating it from the other.
extra_html: Nonlinear electrical transport has recently emerged as an intrinsic property of low-symmetry quantum materials, but the thermoelectric counterpart had not been demonstrated. Kurea Nakagawa, Bart J. van Wees, Marcos H. D. Guimarães and colleagues report it in the type-II Weyl semimetals Td-WTe₂ and TaIrTe₄, using harmonic detection combined with gradient-reversal techniques, and see it persist up to room temperature — with no magnetic field or magnetic material anywhere in the setup. They resolve all symmetry-allowed components of the second-order thermoelectric tensor, including nonlinear Seebeck, nonlinear Nernst and mixed-directional effects, and show that Berry-curvature-related and scattering-induced contributions govern different components. The takeaway they draw is that nonlinear thermoelectricity arises intrinsically from reduced crystal symmetry, opening a route to higher-order heat-to-charge conversion beyond linear response.

related.title: An Electric Field Trick That Nearly Triples Heat Flow
related.hook: Zap a ceramic crystal with an electric field and heat suddenly flows through it almost three times faster in one direction — a jump far beyond anything researchers expected.

related.title: A Material That Remembers How It Radiates Heat
related.hook: Most materials just leak heat the same way forever. This one can be switched between heat-radiating modes with a magnetic field — and it keeps its setting even after the field is gone.

related.title: Semiconductors and the Transistor
related.hook: The entire digital world rests on a tiny switch with no moving parts. The transistor — made from carefully tuned silicon — is the on/off building block behind every chip.

flashcards.prompt: What makes a thermoelectric response 'nonlinear' or nonreciprocal?
flashcards.back_html: A second-order term that does not simply flip sign when the temperature gradient is reversed — so heating from one side is not the mirror image of heating from the other.

flashcards.prompt: What makes the nonlinear thermoelectric effect in these materials 'intrinsic'?

choices.text: It arises from the crystal's own reduced symmetry, with no magnetic field or magnetic material needed
It only appears under a strong applied magnetic field
It requires the sample to be cooled close to absolute zero

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors observed the effect in Td-WTe2 and TaIrTe4 in the absence of magnetic fields or magnetic materials — it follows from the low crystal symmetry itself.

flashcards.prompt: Which two mechanisms govern the different nonlinear thermoelectric components?
flashcards.back_html: Berry-curvature-related contributions and scattering-induced contributions, with each dominating different symmetry-allowed components of the response.
